issues.legal_issue: A revisional authority may not set aside concurrent findings of fact merely because it disagrees with them when the subordinate authorities had jurisdiction and committed no jurisdictional or material procedural error.
material_facts: The subordinate consolidation authorities had jurisdiction to determine whether the revenue entries concerning possession were correct.
Those authorities concurrently found that the recorded tenant possessed the land on his own behalf under a valid lease.
The revisional authority reversed those findings and changed the entries after reassessing the facts, without identifying an error affecting the subordinate authorities’ jurisdiction.
issues.conclusion: The revisional authority exceeded its powers by interfering with the subordinate authorities’ decisions on grounds that did not concern jurisdiction.
issues.legal_principle: Section 48 of the U.P. Consolidation of Holdings Act, 1953, as it stood at the relevant time, was pari materia with section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure. Revision is confined to an inferior authority’s exercise of jurisdiction not vested in it, failure to exercise jurisdiction, or illegal or materially irregular exercise of jurisdiction; it does not permit correction of errors of fact or law unrelated to jurisdiction. The Court relied on Rajah Amir Hassan Khan v. Sheo Baksh Singh, Balakrishna Udayar v. Vasudeva Aiyar, N. S. Venkatagiri Ayyangar v. Hindu Religious Endowments Board, Manindra Land and Building Corporation Ltd. v. Bhutnath Banerjee, Vora Abbashhai Ali-mohammed v. Haji Gulamnabi Haji Safibhai, D.L.F. Housing & Construction Co. Pvt. Ltd. v. Sarup Singh, Pandurang Dhoni Chougute v. Maruti Hari Jadhav, and M. L. Sethi v. R. P. Kapur.

rule.if: revision_proceeding and subordinate_authorities_had_jurisdiction and concurrent_factual_findings and revisional_disagreement_unrelated_to_jurisdiction

predicates.revision_proceeding: A superior authority is reviewing a decision made by a subordinate authority.
predicates.subordinate_authorities_had_jurisdiction: The subordinate authorities were competent to decide the matter before them.
predicates.concurrent_factual_findings: The subordinate authorities reached the same factual conclusion.
predicates.revisional_disagreement_unrelated_to_jur: The reviewing authority disagreed with the subordinate authorities on the merits without identifying a jurisdictional or material procedural defect.

issues.definition: When a superior authority reviews a matter in which competent subordinate authorities made concurrent factual findings, disagreement on the merits alone does not permit it to interfere.

issues.legal_issue: A lease cannot be found fictitious merely because the lessee was related to some purchasers and later transferred the land to a nephew when the transfer’s circumstances and the nephew’s connection to those purchasers are unsupported by evidence.
material_facts: The lessee relied on a registered lease and was recorded as a hereditary tenant; the subordinate authorities found that he possessed the land on his own behalf under that lease.
The revisional authority relied on the lessee’s relationship to three purchasers and a later transfer to his nephew to characterize the lease as fictitious.
The record did not establish when the later transfer occurred, the nephew’s relationship to the purchasers, or the nature of the transfer.
issues.conclusion: The finding that the lease was fictitious could not be sustained on the stated grounds and evidence.
issues.legal_principle: The Court found that the lessee’s relationship to some purchasers did not establish that the lease was fictitious, and that an unexplained later transfer, unsupported by evidence of its timing, nature, or relevant family connection, could not support that finding. The Court also applied the revisional-jurisdiction principle that factual findings of competent subordinate authorities cannot be displaced merely through a different assessment of the facts.

rule.if: land_record_review_proceeding and lease_possession_supported_by_records and relationship_used_to_infer_fiction and later_transfer_details_unsupported

predicates.land_record_review_proceeding: An authority is reviewing records concerning a person's claimed tenancy or possession of land.
predicates.lease_possession_supported_by_records: The person relies on a lease and records of possession, and subordinate decision-makers found possession under that lease.
predicates.relationship_used_to_infer_fiction: The reviewing authority relies on the person's relationship to purchasers as a reason to find the lease fictitious.
predicates.later_transfer_details_unsupported: A later transfer is invoked, but evidence does not establish its timing, nature, or relevant relationship between the transferee and the purchasers.

issues.definition: Where a lease and possession are supported by records, relationship to purchasers and an inadequately evidenced later transfer do not, on their own, support a finding that the lease was fictitious.

issues.legal_issue: A person holding land as a hereditary tenant immediately before vesting is entitled to retain possession as a sirdar and, upon making the required deposit, to a declaration and certificate of bhumidhari rights.
material_facts: The lessee held the land under a valid lease and was in possession on his own behalf.
The revenue records and subordinate authorities’ findings supported his status as a hereditary tenant immediately before the date of vesting.
The Court found no evidence that the lease or the corresponding revenue entries were fictitious or contrary to the actual position.
issues.conclusion: The tenant was entitled to retain possession as a sirdar under section 19 of the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, and, upon the deposit required by sections 134 and 136, was entitled to a declaration and certificate of bhumidhari rights under section 137.
issues.legal_principle: Under sections 19 and 131 of the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950, a hereditary tenant holding land immediately before vesting became entitled to retain possession as a sirdar. Under sections 134 and 136, a sirdar in that class could acquire bhumidhari rights by making the prescribed deposit; section 137 provided for the declaration and certificate. The Court also considered sections 3(28) and 3(9), 6, 7, 18, 20, 134, 135, and 139 in addressing the land-tenure framework, but found it unnecessary to decide the alternative claim to adhivasi rights or the opposing argument concerning section 18.

rule.if: land_tenure_status_determination and valid_lease_possession and hereditary_tenant_immediately_before_vesting and required_deposit_made

predicates.land_tenure_status_determination: A decision determines the land-tenure status arising from a person's holding of land immediately before a change in the land-tenure system.
predicates.valid_lease_possession: The person held the land under a valid lease and possessed it on their own behalf.
predicates.hereditary_tenant_immediately_before_ves: The person held the land as a hereditary tenant immediately before the relevant vesting.
predicates.required_deposit_made: The person made the deposit required to acquire the higher land-tenure status.
predicates.entitled_to_bhumidhar_declaration_and_ce: The person is entitled to a declaration and certificate recognizing the higher land-tenure status.

issues.definition: A person holding land under a valid lease as a hereditary tenant immediately before vesting, who makes the required deposit, is entitled to recognition of bhumidhari rights.
